questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a sign-on flow issues the token
questions.learningObjective: Identify which component issues the token downstream services trust.
questions.stem: A field team signs in to a survey application through a central directory and then calls several downstream services. Which component issues the token that the downstream services trust?

options.text: The central directory issues the token, and downstream services validate it rather than re-authenticating the user.
The survey application issues the token, because it is the first component the user authenticates with.
options.misconception: assumes the first hop the user meets issues the trusted token

options.text: The downstream services issue their own tokens after verifying the user with the directory on every call.
options.misconception: assumes every downstream service performs its own exchange

options.text: The user's device issues the token, so that each service can verify the device without contacting the directory.
options.misconception: assumes a client-side device can mint a token servers trust

questions.explanation: The token is issued where the user authenticates, the central directory. Downstream services validate it against the issuer; re-authenticating per service repeats the exchange the token avoids.
questions.hint: Ask where the user's identity is first established.

questions.stem: A token validator's policy requires 11 checks before it will trust a token, and the implementation currently performs 6 of them. How many required checks are still missing?
questions.explanation: The policy demands 11 checks and the implementation performs 6, so 5 required checks are missing. A validator that skips a required check accepts tokens the policy intended to reject.
questions.hint: Subtract the implemented checks from the required count.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An audience mismatch accepted by a token validator
questions.learningObjective: Explain an audience mismatch defect and what it enables.
questions.stem: A validator accepts tokens whose audience names a different service, and the reviewer wants the reason and the consequence explained in writing. Describe the defect and what it enables.

answer.exemplar: The validator is checking that the token is well formed, is signed by a trusted issuer and has not expired, but it is not checking that the audience claim names the service receiving the token. A token minted for one service can therefore be presented to another and accepted as if it had been issued for it. If the two services hold different levels of trust, the holder of the misdirected token gains the access that belonged to the intended recipient, which is privilege escalation rather than mere misuse of an expired token.

questions.explanation: The audience claim binds a token to the service meant to receive it. If the validator ignores it, a token minted for a low-privilege service can be replayed against a high-privilege one and accepted as genuine.
questions.hint: Ask which service the token was minted for.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Token lifetime against revocation
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a token was rejected using lifetime and skew settings.
questions.stem: A validator is configured with a 15-minute clock skew allowance and a 60-minute token lifetime. A token minted at 09:52 is presented at 10:05 and rejected. What is the reason?

options.text: The token has exceeded its 60-minute lifetime, because the rejection happened after 10:00.
options.misconception: reads the rejection as a lifetime failure without checking the token's age

options.text: The token was minted by the wrong issuer, so the validator refuses tokens issued in the previous hour.
options.misconception: invents an issuer mismatch that no evidence supports

options.text: The clock skew allowance of 15 minutes has already been consumed, so no further leeway remains.
options.misconception: assumes a skew allowance is consumed over time rather than compared

options.text: The token is 13 minutes old, so its lifetime is not the cause; the skew allowance is the setting to examine.

questions.explanation: The token is 13 minutes old against a 60-minute lifetime, so expiry cannot explain the rejection. A skew allowance is a fixed tolerance compared with a timestamp, not a budget spent over time.
questions.hint: Compare the token's age with its lifetime first.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What authenticates a service-to-service call
questions.learningObjective: Determine what authenticates a service-to-service call and what a short-lived identity adds.

stimulus.body: A survey van uploads photos to a storage bucket through a relay. The relay stores a key in a sealed envelope on disk and presents it on every upload. The van's own identity expires every 30 minutes and the field team never sees it.

questions.stem: According to the note, what authenticates the upload, and what does the van's short-lived identity contribute to that upload?

options.text: The van's short-lived identity authenticates the upload, and the stored key is only kept for offline recovery.
options.misconception: treats the expiring identity as the credential that proves the upload

options.text: Both authenticate it independently, since the relay checks the key and the storage service checks the van identity.
options.misconception: assumes both mechanisms independently authenticate the request

options.text: Neither authenticates it, because a sealed envelope on disk is readable by anyone who copies the van's files.
options.misconception: assumes possession of the disk contents defeats the relay's credential

options.text: The stored key authenticates the upload, and the van's short-lived identity only identifies which van is calling.

questions.explanation: The relay proves itself with the stored key, so that authenticates the upload. The van's short-lived identity names the caller for attribution and policy, but it is not the credential storage verifies.
questions.hint: Ask what secret the receiving side actually checks.

questions.topic: The trust a tunnel inherits from its endpoint
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a tunnel's security posture depends on.
questions.stem: First stage: field sensors send readings through a tunnel that terminates at a relay inside the survey station. Second stage: the reviewer asks what the tunnel's security posture depends on.

options.text: It depends on the sensors themselves, because every sensor is required to enforce the tunnel's own controls.
options.misconception: assumes each sensor independently enforces the tunnel's controls

options.text: It depends on the endpoint the tunnel terminates at, since the endpoint enforces the controls the tunnel inherits.
It depends on the encrypted link alone, since a valid link carries the controls regardless of the endpoint.
options.misconception: treats link integrity as a substitute for endpoint enforcement

options.text: It depends on the survey station's staffing, because people at the endpoint enforce the controls.
options.misconception: assumes human staffing at the endpoint is what enforces controls

questions.explanation: A tunnel inherits the posture of the endpoint it terminates at, because that endpoint enforces the controls and admits the traffic. A protected link cannot compensate for an endpoint that admits anything.
questions.hint: Ask where the tunnel's traffic is actually admitted.

options.misconception: assumes network reach replaces the database's own authentication

options.text: It leaves reachability unchanged and simply adds a second path to the database for the field teams.
options.misconception: reads a private endpoint as an added route rather than a restriction

It removes public reachability and also removes the need to review who inside the network is allowed in.
options.misconception: assumes restricting reach removes the need for authorisation inside

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a sign-on flow issues the token
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a token is issued once rather than at each downstream service.
questions.stem: Explain why a token is issued at one point in a sign-on flow rather than at each service the user goes on to reach.

answer.exemplar: Issuing at one point means the user's identity is established once, at the directory, and every later service can verify that single assertion through its signature and the claims it carries. If each service issued its own token, the flow would repeat the authentication exchange for every destination, and each service would have to decide for itself how much the user was authenticated, which is exactly the inconsistency a central token prevents. The cost is that the token must carry enough context for every consumer, since no consumer can ask the directory again.

questions.explanation: One issuance at the directory replaces a fresh exchange at every downstream service. The trade is that the token must carry enough context for all consumers, since none of them can go back and ask the directory again.
questions.hint: Ask what replaces the repeated authentication exchange.

questions.topic: The checks a token validator is still missing
questions.learningObjective: Determine the fraction of required checks a validator enforces.
questions.stem: A validator's policy requires 6 checks. The implementation performs 4 of them, and the two it omits are the audience check and the issuer check. What fraction of the required checks is actually enforced?

options.text: Six of the six are enforced, because the issuer check is implied by verifying the signature.
options.misconception: assumes a verified signature implies the issuer check was performed

options.text: Four of the six are enforced, and the audience and issuer checks can never be enforced anyway.
options.misconception: treats the missing checks as unimplementable rather than unimplemented

options.text: Five of the six are enforced, since the issuer check is enforced while the audience check is not.
options.misconception: miscounts which of the two named checks is performed

options.text: Four of the six required checks are enforced, which is two thirds of the policy.

questions.explanation: The implementation performs 4 of the 6 required checks, which is two thirds of the policy. The omitted checks are audience and issuer, and verifying a signature performs neither of them.
questions.hint: Count the checks performed over the checks required.

questions.topic: An audience mismatch accepted by a token validator

options.text: The acceptance is fine, because both services trust the same directory and therefore share the same trust level.
options.misconception: assumes a shared directory implies identical trust levels

options.text: The token should be shortened instead of rejected, so it cannot be replayed against the second service later.
options.misconception: proposes shortening a token instead of checking its recipient

options.text: The coordinates database should copy the map service's permission checks, so it enforces the same rules.

options.text: The validator must check the audience and reject tokens minted for another service, because the services hold different data.

questions.explanation: A token's audience names its intended service, and these hold different data. The validator must enforce that binding, or a token for public landmarks becomes a key to sensitive nest locations.
questions.hint: Ask which service the token was minted for.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Token lifetime against revocation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how caching changes the revocation guarantee.
questions.stem: First stage: survey tablets cache access tokens for 20 minutes so that a signal loss does not interrupt data entry. Second stage: the security review asks whether caching changes the revocation guarantee.

options.text: Caching does not change the guarantee, because the server checks revocation on every request regardless of the cache.
options.misconception: assumes every request re-checks a revocation list before the cache is used

options.text: Caching widens the window in which a revoked token still works, since the cached copy stays valid until it expires.
Caching removes the revocation guarantee entirely, because an offline copy cannot be withdrawn at all.
options.misconception: claims offline use destroys revocation rather than delaying it

options.text: Caching shortens the effective token lifetime, because the client refreshes it whenever a signal returns.
options.misconception: assumes a cached token expires sooner than its stated lifetime

questions.explanation: Revocation is only effective once the server sees it, and a cached token works until it expires. Caching for 20 minutes extends the window in which a revoked credential is still usable.
questions.hint: Ask how long the cached copy keeps working.

questions.learningObjective: Recall what authenticates a service-to-service call.
questions.stem: A relay calls the survey backend with a key it holds in a sealed envelope. Which statement describes what actually authenticates that call?

options.text: The network path the relay used, because the backend only accepts calls arriving from the station subnet.
options.misconception: treats network location as proof of the calling workload

options.text: The relay's device certificate, because the certificate binds the call to a specific piece of hardware.
options.misconception: assumes a device certificate is presented by a relay holding a sealed key

options.text: The caller's IP address, because it is unique to the relay and therefore identifies it unambiguously.
options.misconception: treats a network address as a unique and verifiable identity

options.text: Possession of the key the relay holds, because the backend verifies that secret and not the network path.

questions.explanation: The backend authenticates the caller by verifying a secret only the relay holds, so possession of that key is what authenticates the call. Network location, address and hardware are context, not proof.
questions.hint: Ask what secret the receiving side checks.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private endpoint removes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: Propose the checks still required after a service moves behind a private endpoint.
questions.stem: Propose what a survey database must still be checked for after it moves behind a private endpoint, and explain what that check covers.

answer.exemplar: The database still needs its own account, role and policy review, because moving it behind a private endpoint only narrows who can open a connection. The check should confirm that every role still maps to the minimum access the field teams need, that the accounts match current personnel, that sign-in records are retained for the required period, and that no service account holds a broader grant than its workflow requires. Reachability and authorisation are separate properties and only one of them changed.

questions.explanation: A private endpoint changes reachability, removing public exposure of the database. It changes no application control, so the accounts, roles and code that decide who may read or write still need their own review.
questions.hint: Ask whether reachability or permission changed.

questions.topic: What a public-read storage policy grants

questions.stem: A storage container holds 500 objects. Its policy makes 320 publicly readable and a further 60 readable by a named survey group. How many objects are not readable by the general public?

options.misconception: double-counts the group objects as excluded and reduces the remainder twice

options.text: Three hundred and twenty are public, so 180 of the 500 objects are not readable by the general public.
Two hundred and sixty are not public, because the group objects are counted as public under the same rule.
options.misconception: assumes the group rule makes its objects publicly readable

questions.hint: Count only the objects the public rule reaches.

Each service would validate one token, and the per-service permissions would be replaced by whatever the token grants.

options.text: It needs nothing further, because a valid signature and live expiry prove the token was meant for the caller.
options.misconception: assumes signature and expiry cover every binding a token needs

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What authenticates a service-to-service call
questions.learningObjective: Explain what authenticates a machine-to-machine call and why the route is not proof.
questions.stem: Explain how the relay in a survey van authenticates to the backend, and why the network path it uses is not part of that proof.

answer.exemplar: The relay proves its identity by presenting the key it holds in the sealed envelope, and the backend verifies that secret against the shared record. The network path contributes context rather than proof: the relay reaches the backend through the station's link, but that path is shared with other devices, traverses infrastructure the relay does not control, and can be observed along the way. A protected route therefore protects the key in transit, but the key is still what the backend actually checks before granting access.

questions.explanation: The backend verifies a secret the relay holds, so that secret is the proof of the calling workload. The route protects that secret in transit and narrows who can reach the backend, but it is not what is checked.
questions.hint: Ask what the backend verifies on arrival.

questions.topic: An audience mismatch accepted by a token validator
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the audience claim and the effect of ignoring it.
questions.stem: A survey archive is protected by a validator that accepts any signed token, and the reviewer asks what the audience claim is for and what happens when it is ignored.

answer.exemplar: The audience claim names the services for which a token was minted, and it is the mechanism that binds one service's credential to another service's endpoint. Without an audience check, a token minted for the archive service can be presented at the recordings endpoint and accepted, because the signature proves only that a trusted issuer produced it. The consequence is that the security of the receiving service now depends on how much the issuing service was trusted to hold, and the two services here were deliberately trusted with different levels of sensitivity.

questions.explanation: The audience claim is the binding between a token and the service that should receive it. Ignoring it lets a token minted for a lower-trust service be replayed at a higher-trust endpoint.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience claim binds together.

options.misconception: miscounts the remaining lifetime and then applies the wrong bound

options.text: The token has 33 minutes left, but the 15-minute skew allowance pushes it over the 60-minute upper bound.
options.misconception: adds the skew allowance to the remaining lifetime before comparing

options.text: The token is rejected because 09:22 is more than 15 minutes past the hour boundary at 09:15.
options.misconception: treats the skew allowance as a limit on time since an hour boundary

options.text: The token has 33 minutes left, inside the accepted band, so the skew allowance is not what decides the outcome.

questions.explanation: A token issued at 09:10 with a 45-minute lifetime expires at 09:55, so at 09:22 it has 33 minutes left, which sits between 5 and 60 minutes and is accepted. The skew allowance is a tolerance for clock disagreement.
questions.hint: Work out the expiry, then the remaining minutes.

The relay would present a token the database checks as a key, so the calls would succeed with a newer credential.
options.misconception: assumes the database treats a token and a key interchangeably

options.text: The relay would present both, so the calls would succeed and the key could be retired safely later.

options.text: The relay would present a token, and the database would accept it because it validates the issuer.
options.misconception: assumes issuer validation is enough for a token-based call

questions.explanation: An authenticator works only if both sides agree, because the verifier decides what counts as proof. Since the database still checks the key, switching to a token replaces a working credential with one the verifier ignores.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a sign-on flow issues the token
questions.learningObjective: Explain where a token should be issued and what it costs.
questions.stem: Explain why issuing the token at the directory rather than at each downstream service matters for a survey deployment, and name the cost of that choice.

answer.exemplar: Issuing at the directory establishes the user's identity once and lets every downstream service verify that single assertion, which matters most in the field where the satellite link is congested and repeated exchanges cost real time. The cost is that the token must carry every piece of context any consumer might need, because a consumer that finds the token insufficient cannot simply go back and ask the directory. Claims therefore tend to grow, and every consumer must be able to ignore the claims meant for someone else.

questions.explanation: Central issuance removes a repeated exchange at every service, which matters when the link is slow. The cost is that the token must carry context for all consumers, which must ignore claims meant for others.
questions.hint: Ask what the token must now carry for everyone.

options.misconception: invents an overlap between two rules that address different objects

questions.explanation: A grant scoped to a named group is not a grant to the world, so the public reach is the 300 objects under the public rule alone. The 120 group objects are separate objects reached by a restricted rule.
questions.hint: Ask which rule the general public satisfies.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private endpoint removes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a private endpoint does not replace application access controls.
questions.stem: Explain why moving a service behind a private endpoint is not a substitute for the service's own access controls, and describe the residual risk it leaves.

answer.exemplar: A private endpoint changes the set of callers who can open a connection, so it removes the internet-facing exposure of the service. It does not touch the accounts, roles or policies the service enforces on callers who do connect, and anyone inside the network, including a compromised laptop in the survey station, can still reach the service. The residual risk is therefore insider or lateral movement inside the trusted boundary, which is exactly the population the service's own authentication and authorisation controls exist to constrain.

questions.explanation: A private endpoint restricts who can open a connection but leaves the service's authentication, roles and policies untouched. Hosts inside the boundary can still reach it, so those controls remain necessary.
questions.hint: Ask who inside the boundary can still connect.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What authenticates a service-to-service call
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a stored secret authenticates better than a network address.
questions.stem: Explain why a sealed key on the relay disk authenticates a service-to-service call more reliably than the relay's network address does.

answer.exemplar: The sealed key is a secret that only the relay holds and that the backend can verify directly, so possession of it is what the backend actually checks before granting access. The network address is not a secret and not a proof: it can be observed along the route, it may be reused by another device on the same segment, and it says nothing about the process making the request. The address is useful for routing and for coarse policy, while the key is what binds the call to the specific workload.

questions.explanation: The key is a verifiable secret only the relay holds, so the backend checks it directly and ties the call to that workload. An address is observable, shareable and proves nothing about the calling process.
questions.hint: Ask what the backend can verify.

stimulus.body: The relay calls two backends: the species catalogue over a link inside the station, and the regional archive over a cellular link. The note records that the species catalogue accepts a sealed key from the relay, while the regional archive expects a client certificate that the relay presents from its own store.

questions.stem: Given the note, what authenticates each call, and what do the two mechanisms have in common?

options.text: The catalogue call is authenticated by the network location, and the archive call by the certificate the relay stores.
options.misconception: treats a link inside the station as proof of the calling workload

options.text: The catalogue call is authenticated by its stored key, and the archive call by the address of the cellular link.
options.misconception: substitutes a network address for the credential the archive checks

options.text: Each is authenticated by a credential the relay holds and presents; in both cases the proof is possession, not location.
Neither call is authenticated by a credential, since both rely on the cellular or station link being trustworthy.
options.misconception: assumes the transport alone authenticates the caller

questions.explanation: Each backend verifies something the relay possesses, a shared key or a certificate, and possession is what the check establishes. The link proves nothing about the calling workload.
questions.hint: Ask what each backend actually verifies.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The trust a tunnel inherits from its endpoint
questions.learningObjective: State what a tunnel's protection actually consists of.
questions.stem: First stage: a tunnel from the field to the survey station terminates at a relay whose controls cover only network admission. Second stage: the reviewer asks what the tunnel's protection actually consists of.

options.text: It is the tunnel's own end-to-end encryption, because the relay's admission controls are only the first hop.
options.misconception: assumes the tunnel adds protections beyond its endpoint and link

options.text: It is the relay's admission controls plus the link's protection, since neither the tunnel nor the sensors add more.
It is the relay's admission controls alone, because the link between the field and the station is trusted.
options.misconception: assumes the long link between field and station is trusted by default

options.text: It is the sensors' local encryption, because the relay merely forwards what it receives.
options.misconception: credits the sensors with the tunnel's protections

questions.explanation: The tunnel's protection is the sum of the endpoint's admission controls and whatever the link provides. Neither the tunnel nor the sensors contribute enforcement, so the relay's posture is decisive.
questions.hint: Add up what the endpoint and the link provide.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private endpoint removes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: State what a private endpoint changes and what it leaves in place.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes what a private endpoint changes and what it leaves in place for the service behind it?

options.text: It changes who can open a connection, and leaves the service's own authentication, roles and records exactly as they were.
It changes who can connect and also replaces the service's authentication with network-level identity.
options.misconception: assumes network reach substitutes for the service's authentication

options.text: It changes nothing about access and simply removes the service's address from public listings.
options.misconception: reads the endpoint as an address hiding measure rather than a restriction

options.text: It changes who can connect and also makes the service's own role definitions unnecessary.
options.misconception: assumes restricting reach removes the need for role design

questions.explanation: A private endpoint is a network restriction on who may open a connection, and it says nothing about the service's own controls. Accounts, roles and sign-in records must still be designed and reviewed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the service's own checks changed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a public-read storage policy grants
questions.learningObjective: Count the objects left outside public reach under a proportional policy.
questions.stem: A bucket policy grants public read to 40 percent of 250 objects in a store. How many objects are not publicly readable?
questions.explanation: Forty percent of 250 objects is 100 objects that are publicly readable, so 250 minus 100 leaves 150 that the general public cannot read under the policy.
questions.hint: Work out the publicly readable count and subtract it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a sign-on flow issues the token
questions.learningObjective: Justify where a token should be issued and what evidence confirms it.
questions.stem: Explain how a sign-on flow should decide where the token is issued, and what evidence shows the choice was right.

answer.exemplar: The token should be issued by the component that performed the authentication, because that is the only place where the assurance actually exists, and every other component should validate the resulting token rather than repeat the exchange. Evidence that the choice was right appears in the operational record: a drop in directory lookups per session, fewer timeouts on the congested link, and a token whose claims are few enough that each consumer can state exactly which ones it reads.

questions.explanation: The issuer should be the component that verified the user; everyone else validates the token rather than repeating the exchange. Evidence appears as fewer directory lookups, fewer timeouts and a smaller claim set.
questions.hint: Ask which component actually performed the check.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The checks a token validator is still missing
questions.learningObjective: Determine the enforcement rate of required checks across a validator fleet.
questions.stem: Across 6 validators, each policy requires 5 checks, and 4 of them are implemented on each validator. What fraction of the required checks across the fleet is actually enforced?

options.text: Twenty-four of thirty required checks are enforced, which is four fifths of the fleet's requirement.
All thirty checks are enforced, because the two omitted checks are covered by the signature verification.
options.misconception: assumes a verified signature substitutes for the omitted checks

options.text: Four of six checks per validator are enforced, giving an enforcement rate of just under two thirds.
options.misconception: computes the rate from one validator and misstates it as the fleet's

options.text: Twenty checks are enforced across the fleet, because the omitted checks count only once.
options.misconception: counts the omitted checks once instead of once per validator

questions.explanation: Each of the 6 validators needs 5 checks, so the fleet requires 30, and 4 implemented on each gives 24 enforced. That is four fifths of the requirement, not the per-validator fraction.
questions.hint: Total the requirement across the fleet, then divide.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An audience mismatch accepted by a token validator
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the root cause of an accepted token and name the fix.

stimulus.body: An audit of the coordinates service found that the validator accepted a token minted for the archive service, and the archive was known to be a lower-trust component. The note also recorded that the validator had no way to list the services it was willing to accept, because the tokens carried no audience claim at all.

questions.stem: According to the note, what is the root cause of the acceptance, and what change would close it?

options.text: The validator's signature check is too permissive, so it accepts tokens minted by the archive service.
options.misconception: blames signature verification for a missing audience claim

options.text: The tokens carry no audience claim, so the validator cannot bind a token to a service; the claim must be added and checked.
The archive service is trusted too widely, so the fix is to lower its trust level in the directory.
options.misconception: treats a claim problem as a directory trust configuration problem

options.text: The coordinates service holds too much data, so the fix is to move it behind a private endpoint.
options.misconception: proposes a network control for a token binding problem

questions.explanation: Without an audience claim there is nothing for a validator to compare against the receiving service, so acceptance is unavoidable. The fix is to issue tokens with an audience and check it at every validator.
questions.hint: Ask what the validator has to compare against.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Token lifetime against revocation
questions.learningObjective: Bound the exposure that token lifetime and revocation settings provide.
questions.stem: First stage: a service issues 30-minute access tokens and keeps a revocation list that consumers refresh every 2 minutes. Second stage: the reviewer asks what the pair of settings actually guarantees.

options.text: A revoked token can never be used again, because the list is refreshed every 2 minutes.
options.misconception: ignores the delay between publication and the refresh of the list

options.text: A revoked token can be used for the rest of its 30-minute lifetime, because the list applies only to new tokens.
options.misconception: assumes revocation never applies to tokens already issued

options.text: A revoked token can be used for up to 30 minutes, since the refresh interval only affects new token issuance.
options.misconception: misreads the refresh interval as having no effect on live tokens

options.text: A revoked token can still be used for up to 2 minutes of list staleness, and no longer than its remaining lifetime.

questions.explanation: Revocation reaches consumers when they refresh the list, so a revoked token survives for up to the refresh interval and never beyond its remaining lifetime. The settings bound exposure rather than remove it.
questions.hint: Bound the exposure with both settings together.
